GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: The showers and thunderstorms will taper off Friday as drier air moves in from the southwest.
GJT.text: High pressure over the Gulf drifting west into Mexico and a deep low currently off the Oregon Coast descending south off the West Coast will dominate the weather pattern through the rest of the week and possibly into early next week. The current southwesterly flow is pulling Pacific moisture up through Southern California and the Desert Southwest into the region that supported weak isolated light showers with a few thunderstorms today, and will again tomorrow, but coverage does look to be a little more isolated. As the low bottoms out off the Southern California Coast by Wednesday morning, turning to the northeast to track up across the Great Basin and Utah by Friday, the High pressure moves in over northeastern Mexico to set up a more southerly flow than we saw with the last tropical surge of moisture. This scenario sets the deeper plume of tropical moisture from the remnants of Hurricane Trudy to plow into the southern mountains where current guidance has the bulk of the rain falling, and casting a rain shadow to the north in the central and northern mountains. This being said, there is still a lot of uncertainty creeping into the forecast as early as Wednesday. The latest guidance is sliding the moist plume to the west a bit that would allow more moisture to push north into southern Utah and to the east into the central and northern Colorado areas. The Atmospheric River (AR) models do support this solution with Integrated Vapor Transport (IVT) values up to 500 kg/m/s pushing into the central and northern areas. As a result, storm totals have increased to one to two inches rain in the central mountains and up to an inch farther north. Mean while the southern face of the San Juan and Abajo Mountains will see two to three inches rain with locally higher amounts possible. This system is a very warm system with snow levels remaining above 12K ft through Thursday creating a risk for receiving rain on snow through the southern mountains that can lead to high stream flow

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: There is some more agreement for this package on the evolution of the trough for Friday and beyond.
BOU.text:
There have been only minimal changes to the forecast over the last 24 hours. The Denver metro and the plains will see high temperatures in the 70s through the week with high temperatures even pushing 80 on the eastern plains for Wednesday and Thursday. Some record warm minimums are possible for Denver towards the end of the week as cloud cover increases.

Radar over the last several hours has shown some isolated to scattered rain/snow showers for the mountains, but there is almost no precipitation left at this hour. An upper-level ridge builds into eastern Colorado on Tuesday and Wednesday with our area on the periphery of it and some drier air filtering in. Wednesday and Friday should be the warmest days of the week ahead. Rain chances start to decrease, even compared to the relatively low chances we had on Monday. Tuesday only brings the chance for isolated rain/snow showers for the mountains. The coverage drops to near zero on Wednesday until late in the afternoon. Almost no accumulation is expected through at least 18z Wednesday. By Wednesday afternoon, more widespread showers should start to approach our southwestern counties.

The overall synoptic pattern forecast through Friday generally remains the same as noted in previous discussions. An upper-level low over the Pacific Ocean should approach California on Wednesday, move inland, and be centered over Utah by Friday morning. Southwest flow aloft looks to continue through the week for our area with moisture starting to increase on Wednesday. Some moisture associated with what is now Tropical Storm Trudy gets pulled into the flow aloft and funneled into southwest Colorado for late Wednesday through Friday. The vast majority of the precipitation for our area should stay in the high country, but there is a a low chance a couple of showers could move onto the plains late Thursday. PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Further east, with the transitory ridge, warm and mainly dry conditions will be in place, with chances of showers spreading east across the plains in later Thursday, as the Pacific system lifts out across the Northern Rockies.
PUB.text:
Latest operational and ensemble model data remain in good agreement through the end of the work week, with transitory upper ridging building across eastern Colorado through Thursday, as southwest flow increases across western Colorado ahead of an eastern Pacific storm system digging into the Great Basin. Model data supports abundant sup-tropical moisture becoming entrained within the southwest flow aloft, with PWATS of 0.8 to over 1 inch (200-300 percent of normal) moving across the region in the Wednesday and Thursday timeframe. This, along with increasing orographic flow, and uvv associated with the Pacific system moving across the Great Basin, will lead to increasing coverage and intensity of precipitation along and west of the Continental Divide Wednesday, with the heaviest precipitation expected Thursday into Thursday night, as the main system starts to lift out across the Great Basin into the Northern Rockies.

Latest model data continues to support qpf of 1 to 3 inches along and west of the ContDvd through this period, with probabilities of >3 inches of liquid qpf in the 60 to 80 percent range across the San Juan Mtns. The Pacific origin of the system is expected to keep snow levels around peak level (at and above 12,000 feet) through the duration of the heavy precipitation event (at least through Thursday night), leading to concerns of river and stream flooding as well as the potential for rock/mudslides across the higher terrain of the ContDvd. However, the area of greatest concern remains across the San Juan Mtns, with already saturated soils from previous precipitation last week, as well the potential for rain on top of snowpack already in place, with SNOTEL data indicating SWE 3/4 to 1" across the San Juans at this time. Stay tuned for more information on this potentially high impact event unfolding later this week, with Flood Watches likely being issued as we get closer in time to this heavy precipitation event.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Sunday/Monday...Drier conditions return under northwest flow aloft and as the low and mid levels dry out somewhat. 700 mb temperatures near 3 Celsius will yield high temperatures in the mid 50s to lower 60s.
CYS.text:
Wednesday...Westerly flow aloft continues and with dry low and mid levels, no precipitation is expected.

Thursday...Moist south southwest flow aloft develops in advance of the upper low over Nevada, with deeper moisture and a weak shortwave trough aloft moving across our western counties, producing scattered showers and a few thunderstorms south of a line from Rawlins, to Wheatland to Cheyenne.

Friday...As the main trough aloft moves across western Wyoming, a cold front will lie north to south across our counties, helping to produce scattered showers mainly west of I-25 in the afternoon, and spreading eastward in the evening.

Saturday...The primary trough aloft moves overhead early in the day, and orographic lift will likely produce scattered showers in the afternoon from Douglas to Laramie, and in the evening south of a Rawlins to Scottsbluff line.

Sunday/Monday...Drier conditions return under northwest flow aloft and as the low and mid levels dry out somewhat. 700 mb temperatures near 3 Celsius will yield high temperatures in the mid 50s to lower 60s.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: While forecast confidence heading into the weekend is still low, model guidance suggests warmer and drier weather to come.
SLC.text:
Satellite imagery this afternoon and evening has been visually impressive as a strong closed low circulates and moves southward off of the west coast. This system continues to be the main story in Utah's weather through the work week. Late this evening, isolated showers will develop primarily across higher terrain and the northern Wasatch Front, but will be largely unimpactful with little to no QPF expected.

As the aforementioned closed low begins to inch closer late Tuesday, increasing southwest flow will draw moisture of tropical origins northward into southern Utah. Alongside upper-level diffluence and jet support, precipitation chances will increase, particularly early Wednesday morning across southern Utah. Models have trended earlier with the onset of this precipitation, with more widespread showers beginning after 6AM Wednesday across the south, expanding into northern Utah as early as mid-afternoon.

Thunderstorms on Wednesday have the potential to be a bit more organized across southern Utah. Given a favorable environment with better instability, moisture, and shear in place ahead of the approaching system, gusty winds and hail will be the main threats. However, with southeasterly to easterly surface flow veering to southwesterly not far above the surface, a tornado cannot be ruled out, especially considering low LCLs.

Widespread precipitation will continue through Thursday as the closed low slowly pushes eastward. Flash flooding will remain a threat, particularly for prone areas such as slot canyons and dry washes. By Friday morning, cold air will push into the state as the trough axis passes overhead. Snow levels will drop to 7500-9000ft as 700-mb temperatures dip to -3C to -6C by late Friday. As such, snow accumulations of 3-6 inches above 9000ft across the northern mountains are expected, with perhaps a bit more across higher elevations in the Wasatch and Uintas.

BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Pattern uncertainty increases behind this system, however Saturday at the very least should be dry with temperatures warming to near normal again.
BOI.text:
Widespread showers will be the story Thursday into Friday, as the low lifts northeast over our area from California. While cloud cover will help limit daytime instability, cooling aloft will allow for weak instability to develop, resulting in a slight chance of embedded thunderstorms. Any thunderstorms will result in localized heavier rainfall rates/totals underneath the core. At least for Thursday, southerly flow aloft will keep snow levels on the higher side (9-10kft MSL), giving rain its opportunity to shine as the dominate precipitation type. Over the course of Thursday through Friday, guidance continues to trend upwards on total accumulations, with lower elevations ranging from 0.15-0.50 inches (lowest in eastern Oregon), mountain valleys ranging from 0.50-0.80 inches, and highest elevations up to 1.25 inches; with the bulk of the precipitation falling late Thursday into early Friday. While this will be more stratiform and long duration in nature, steep terrain/burn scars may experience increased runoff and land movement.

A cold front on Friday will bring a rather sharp end to the precip and a cooldown as it moves across our area from west to east. Temperatures comes Friday will drop around 5 degrees below normal. Another, probably more notable, consequence of the cold front will be the gusty west-northwest winds that will accompany it. Friday afternoon, winds across ridge tops and open terrain will gust to 20- 35 mph. The strongest winds, however, will blow in the Snake River Plain east of Mountain Home where gusts will reach 35-45 mph. Lowering snow levels on Friday behind the front will allow for a transition to snow/wintry mix for elevations above 6.5 kft MSL. Although this switch will be at the tail end of the precipitation, so only a dusting of snow is expected along high elevation passes such as Banner Summit.
